Main.sentence: James David Vance (born James Donald Bowman , [a] August 2, 1984) is an American politician, author, attorney, and ___E:Marine Corps U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Marine_Corps)___ veteran who is the 50th ___E:vice president of the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_president_of_the_United_States)___ .

A member of the ___E:Republican Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States))___ , he represented ___E:Ohio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio)___ in the ___E:U.S. Senate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate)___ from 2023 to 2025. During ___E:his tenure as vice president U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_presidency_of_JD_Vance)___ , Vance has also served as the finance chair of the ___E:Republican National Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_National_Committee)___ .
Born and raised in ___E:Middletown, Ohio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middletown,_Ohio)___ , Vance served in the U.S.
Marine Corps and deployed to the ___E:Iraq War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War)___ as a ___E:military journalist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_journalist)___ .

He earned a bachelor's degree from ___E:Ohio State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_State_University)___ and a law degree from ___E:Yale Law School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_Law_School)___ .

After briefly working as a corporate lawyer and Senate aide, Vance became a venture capitalist at ___E:Peter Thiel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Thiel)___ 's ___E:Mithril Capital U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mithril_Capital)___ .
In 2016, he published Hillbilly Elegy , a bestselling memoir that brought him national attention.

After ___E:initially opposing Donald Trump's candidacy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Never_Trump_movement#Former_Never_Trumpers)___ in the ___E:2016 election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election)___ , Vance became a strong Trump supporter during ___E:Trump's first presidency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump%27s_first_presidency)___ .

He won the ___E:2022 United States Senate election in Ohio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_United_States_Senate_election_in_Ohio)___ , beating ___E:Democratic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ nominee ___E:Tim Ryan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Ryan_(Ohio_politician))___ .

Vance ___E:served as Ohio's senator U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Senate_career_of_JD_Vance)___ from January 2023 to January 2025. In July 2024, ___E:Trump selected Vance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Republican_Party_vice_presidential_candidate_selection)___ as his running mate before the ___E:Republican National Convention U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Republican_National_Convention)___ .

Trump and Vance won the ___E:2024 United States presidential election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election)___ , defeating Democratic nominees ___E:Kamala Harris U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris)___ and ___E:Tim Walz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Walz)___ .

Vance is the first ___E:millennial U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millennial)___ and the ___E:third-youngest vice president in U.S. history U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_vice_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_age)___ .

He has been characterized as a ___E:national conservative U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_conservative)___ and ___E:right-wing populist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right-wing_populist)___ , and describes himself as a member of the ___E:postliberal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postliberalism)___ right. ___E:His political positions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_positions_of_JD_Vance)___ include opposition to ___E:abortion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_in_the_United_States)___ , ___E:same-sex marriage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage_in_the_United_States)___ , and ___E:gun control U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_control)___ .

Vance is an outspoken critic of ___E:childlessness U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Childlessness)___ and has acknowledged the ___E:influence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church_in_the_United_States)___ of ___E:Catholic theology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_theology)___ on his sociopolitical positions.
He is the second vice president to serve under a president who won a non-consecutive second term. [b]
Vance was born James Donald Bowman on August 2, 1984, in ___E:Middletown, Ohio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middletown,_Ohio)___ ,   where he was also raised.
His mother is Beverly Carol Aikins (née Vance), and his father was Donald Ray Bowman;  they divorced when he was a toddler.
Vance wrote in his book Hillbilly Elegy that he was of Scots-Irish descent.

He grew up in an ___E:Appalachian American U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_American)___ culture, spending summers with relatives in ___E:Jackson, Kentucky U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Kentucky)___ .

After he was adopted by his mother's third husband, Bob Hamel, his mother changed his name to James David Hamel to remove his biological father's first name and surname and to use an uncle's first name, David.
Vance therefore kept his first name and his nickname, JD. His surname eventually changed to her maiden name after her parents became his caretakers.
Vance has written that his childhood was marked by poverty and abuse, and that his mother struggled with ___E:drug addiction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_addiction)___ .
He and his elder sister, Lindsay, were raised primarily by their maternal grandparents, James and Bonnie Vance (née Blanton), whom they called "Papaw" and "Mamaw".
During ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ , Vance's uncle Samuel T. Blanton and great-grandfather Blaine Blanton both served in the U.S.
Navy in the ___E:Pacific Theatre of Operations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Theatre_of_Operations)___ and in ___E:Japan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan)___ .

After graduating from ___E:Middletown High School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middletown_High_School_(Ohio))___ in 2003, Vance enlisted in the ___E:United States Marine Corps U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Marine_Corps)___ ,  serving as a combat correspondent ( ___E:military journalist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_journalist)___ ) with the ___E:2nd Marine Aircraft Wing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_Marine_Aircraft_Wing)___ .

During his four years of service, he was deployed to the ___E:Iraq War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War)___ in 2005 for six months in a non-combat role, writing articles and taking photographs.

He attained the rank of ___E:corporal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal#United_States)___ , and his decorations included the ___E:Marine Corps Good Conduct Medal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Corps_Good_Conduct_Medal)___ and the ___E:Navy and Marine Corps Achievement Medal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navy_and_Marine_Corps_Achievement_Medal)___ .

In 2007, Vance left the military and used the ___E:G.I. Bill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G.I._Bill)___   to study at ___E:Ohio State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_State_University)___ .
He graduated in 2009 with a ___E:Bachelor of Arts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts)___ (BA) degree summa cum laude in political science and philosophy.
In 2010, Vance entered ___E:Yale Law School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_Law_School)___ ,  where he won a prestigious position on The Yale Law Journal .
During his first year, Professor ___E:Amy Chua U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amy_Chua)___ persuaded Vance to begin writing his memoir, Hillbilly Elegy .

Vance also initiated a rapport with ___E:Peter Thiel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Thiel)___ after attending his 2011 talk at Yale.  In 2010–2011, Vance wrote for ___E:David Frum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Frum)___ 's "FrumForum" website under the name J. D.
Hamel.

Although Hillbilly Elegy states that he adopted his grandparents' surname of Vance upon his marriage in 2014,   the name change actually occurred in April 2013, as he was about to graduate from Yale.   Vance obtained his ___E:Juris Doctor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juris_Doctor)___ (JD) degree from Yale Law School in May 2013.
After graduating from law school, Vance worked for Republican senator ___E:John Cornyn U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cornyn)___ .

He spent a year as a ___E:law clerk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_clerk)___ for Judge ___E:David Bunning U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bunning)___ of the ___E:U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._District_Court_for_the_Eastern_District_of_Kentucky)___ ,  then worked at the law firm ___E:Sidley Austin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidley_Austin)___ ,  beginning a brief career as a ___E:corporate lawyer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_lawyer)___ .

Having practiced law for slightly under two years, Vance moved to San Francisco to work in the technology industry as a ___E:venture capitalist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capitalist)___ .
Between 2016 and 2017, he served as a principal at Peter Thiel's firm, ___E:Mithril Capital U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mithril_Capital)___ .
In June 2016, ___E:Harper U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper_(publisher))___ published Vance's book, Hillbilly Elegy: A Memoir of a Family and Culture in Crisis .
The memoir recounts the ___E:Appalachian culture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_culture)___ and socioeconomic problems of Vance's small-town upbringing.

Hillbilly Elegy was on ___E:The New York Times Best Seller list U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times_Best_Seller_list)___ in ___E:2016 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times_Non-Fiction_Best_Sellers_of_2016)___ and ___E:2017 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times_Non-Fiction_Best_Sellers_of_2017)___ .

The Times listed it among "6 Books to Help Understand Trump's Win",  and Vance was profiled in The Washington Post , which called him "the voice of the ___E:Rust Belt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_Belt)___ ".

In The New Republic , Sarah Jones criticized Vance as "liberal media's favorite ___E:white trash U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_trash)___ –splainer" and a "false prophet of ___E:blue America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_America)___ ", calling the book "little more than a list of myths about ___E:welfare queens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_queen)___ ".
Hillbilly Elegy ' s success helped propel Vance into contact with social elites, and he began writing a column for The New York Times .
Vance later said that his interactions with social elites from this time, particularly their perceived disdain for "the people he grew up with", helped shape his later views.
In 2017, Vance joined ___E:Revolution LLC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolution_LLC)___ ,  an investment firm founded by ___E:Steve Case U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Case)___ .

Vance was tasked with expanding the "Rise of the Rest" initiative, which focuses on growing investments in underserved regions outside ___E:Silicon Valley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley)___ and New York City.

Vance was a ___E:CNN U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN)___ contributor in 2017 and 2018.  In April 2017, ___E:Ron Howard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Howard)___ signed on to direct ___E:the film version U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillbilly_Elegy_(film))___ of Hillbilly Elegy , which was released in select theaters on November 11, 2020, and later that month on ___E:Netflix U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix)___ for streaming.

The film was nominated for two ___E:Academy Awards U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/93rd_Academy_Awards)___ and two ___E:Screen Actors Guild Awards U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/27th_Screen_Actors_Guild_Awards)___ ,   among others.

In 2019, Vance served on the board of advisors of the ___E:With Honor Fund U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/With_Honor_Fund)___ , a ___E:Super PAC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_action_committee#Super_PACs)___ that helps veterans run for office.

From 2020 to 2023, he served on the board of advisors of American Moment, a networking and training organization for young conservatives that is affiliated with ___E:Project 2025 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_2025)___ .

In 2019, Vance and ___E:Chris Buskirk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Buskirk)___ co-founded the conservative political advocacy group ___E:Rockbridge Network U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockbridge_Network)___ .

That year, he also co-founded venture capital firm Narya Capital in Cincinnati with financial backing from Thiel, ___E:Eric Schmidt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Schmidt)___ , and ___E:Marc Andreessen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Andreessen)___ .

During 2020, he raised $93 million for the firm.  With ___E:Peter Thiel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Thiel)___ and former Trump adviser Darren Blanton, Vance invested in ___E:Rumble U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumble_(website))___ , a Canadian ___E:online video platform U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_video_platform)___ popular with the political right.
In December 2016, Vance said he planned to move to Ohio and would consider starting a nonprofit or running for office.

In Ohio, he started Our Ohio Renewal, a ___E:501(c)(4) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/501(c)(4))___ advocacy organization focused on education, addiction, and other "social ills" he had mentioned in his memoir.

According to a 2017 archived capture of the nonprofit's website, the advisory board members were ___E:Keith Humphreys U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Humphreys)___ , ___E:Jamil Jivani U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Jivani)___ , ___E:Yuval Levin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuval_Levin)___ , and ___E:Sally Satel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Satel)___ .
According to a 2020 capture of the website, those four remained in those positions throughout the organization's existence.
Our Ohio Renewal closed by 2021 with sparse achievements.
According to Jivani, the organization's director of law and policy, its work was derailed by Jivani's ___E:cancer diagnosis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lymphoma)___ .
It raised around $221,000 in 2017 (including $80,000 from Vance himself) and spent most of its revenue on ___E:overhead costs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overhead_costs)___ and travel.
In subsequent years, it raised less than $50,000.
During Vance's 2022 U.S.
Senate campaign, ___E:Tim Ryan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Ryan_(Ohio_politician))___ , the Democratic nominee, said the charity was a front for Vance's political ambitions.
Ryan pointed to reports that the organization paid a Vance political adviser and conducted public opinion polling, while its efforts to address addiction failed.

Vance denied the characterization.   [c] Our Ohio Renewal's tax filings show that in its first year, it spent more (over $63,000) on "management services" provided by its executive director ___E:Jai Chabria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jai_Chabria)___ , who also served as Vance's top political adviser, than it did on programs to fight opioid abuse.

In 2017, Vance formed a similarly named ___E:501(c)(3) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/501(c)_organization#501(c)(3))___ organization, Our Ohio Renewal Foundation, which raised around $69,000 from 2017 to 2023.  As of September 2024, the foundation had not spent any funds since 2019.

According to the ___E:Associated Press U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press)___ (AP) and a 2019 ___E:ProPublica U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ProPublica)___ investigation, the charity's biggest accomplishment, sending psychiatrist ___E:Sally Satel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Satel)___ to Ohio's Appalachian region for a yearlong residency in 2018, was "tainted" by the ties among Satel, her employer, ___E:American Enterprise Institute U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Enterprise_Institute)___ (AEI), and ___E:Purdue Pharma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purdue_Pharma)___ , in the form of knowledge exchange between Satel and Purdue and financial support from Purdue to AEI. Satel denied having any relationship with Purdue or any knowledge of its donations to AEI.

From March 2017 to April 2021, Vance served on the board of directors of the startup ___E:AppHarvest U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AppHarvest)___ , which carried out indoor ___E:vertical farming U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertical_farming)___ in Kentucky.

AppHarvest was also one of Narya Capital's first publicly announced investments; Vance publicly advocated for AppHarvest, touting the company's commitment to bring good jobs with health care benefits to an economically depressed area of Appalachia.
AppHarvest went bankrupt in 2023 while owing over $340 million.
Company founder Jonathan Webb and top executives collectively had little experience with horticulture and indoor agriculture, and the company struggled to meet its produce buyers' standards.

Workers complained to authorities about "brutal" working conditions in company greenhouses; after many local workers quit, they were replaced by migrant contract workers, who eventually constituted over half the company's labor force.

Vance never held an operational role at the company, and his vice-presidential campaign said he had been unaware of the complaints about working conditions and that the decision to hire migrants was made after he resigned from the board.

In early 2018, Vance considered running for the ___E:U.S. Senate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate)___ against ___E:Sherrod Brown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherrod_Brown)___ ,  but did not.  In March 2021, ___E:Peter Thiel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Thiel)___ gave $10 million to Protect Ohio Values, a ___E:super PAC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_PAC)___ created in February to support a potential Vance candidacy.    ___E:Robert Mercer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mercer)___ also gave an undisclosed amount.
In April, Vance expressed interest in running for the Senate seat being vacated by ___E:Rob Portman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Portman)___ .
In May, he launched an ___E:exploratory committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exploratory_committee)___ .

Vance announced his Senate campaign in Ohio on July 1, 2021.  On May 3, 2022, he won the Republican primary with 32% of the vote,  defeating multiple candidates, including ___E:Josh Mandel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josh_Mandel)___ (23%) and ___E:Matt Dolan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Dolan)___ (22%).

On November 8, in the general election, Vance defeated ___E:Democratic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ nominee ___E:Tim Ryan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Ryan_(Ohio_politician))___ with 53% of the vote to Ryan's 47%.

This vote share was considered a vast underperformance compared to other Ohio Republicans, especially in the ___E:coinciding gubernatorial election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Ohio_gubernatorial_election)___ .

Vance had often previously spelled his name with periods after his initials ("J.D.")—including in the publication of Hillbilly Elegy —but after becoming a candidate for office, he removed the periods ("JD").
On January 3, 2023, Vance was sworn into the Senate as a member of the ___E:118th United States Congress U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/118th_United_States_Congress)___ .

Vance served as Ohio's junior senator from January 3, 2023, to January 3, 2025. Data from mid-July 2024 showed that he had made 45 Senate speeches and sponsored 57 legislative bills, none of which had passed the Senate.
Vance had also co-sponsored 288 bills, of which two passed both the Senate and the House but were vetoed by President Biden.

On March 1, 2023, Vance and Senator ___E:Sherrod Brown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherrod_Brown)___ co-sponsored bipartisan legislation to prevent derailments like the one in ___E:East Palestine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Palestine,_Ohio,_train_derailment)___ ,   but the bill failed due to lack of intra-caucus Republican support.

In June 2023, Vance voted against raising the debt ceiling, standing against final passage of the ___E:Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiscal_Responsibility_Act_of_2023)___  and saying it would result in "a reduced military in the face of a rising threat from China".

In July 2023, Vance and Representative ___E:Marjorie Taylor Greene U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marjorie_Taylor_Greene)___ introduced legislation that would have made ___E:gender-affirming care U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender-affirming_care)___ for minors a federal crime, with penalties of up to 12 years in prison.

In June 2024, Vance sponsored the Dismantle DEI Act, which would ban federal ___E:diversity, equity, and inclusion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diversity,_equity,_and_inclusion)___ programs and funding for agencies, contractors, and organizations receiving federal funds.
Vance was not present for any Senate votes during his vice-presidential campaign.
Vance became Ohio's senior senator on January 3, 2025, upon the swearing-in of ___E:Bernie Moreno U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Moreno)___ .

At midnight on January 10, Vance resigned from the Senate in anticipation of his inauguration as ___E:vice president of the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_president_of_the_United_States)___ on ___E:January 20 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_inauguration_of_Donald_Trump)___ .

On January 17, Governor ___E:Mike DeWine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_DeWine)___ announced his appointment of ___E:Jon Husted U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Husted)___ to the Senate seat Vance vacated.

On January 31, 2023, Vance endorsed former president Donald Trump in the ___E:2024 Republican Party presidential primaries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries)___ .

On July 15, 2024, the first day of the ___E:Republican National Convention U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Republican_National_Convention)___ , Trump announced on ___E:Truth Social U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truth_Social)___ that he had chosen Vance as his running mate.  On July 17, the third day of the convention, Vance accepted the nomination to be Trump's running mate.

Along with Vance, North Dakota governor ___E:Doug Burgum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doug_Burgum)___ , Florida senator ___E:Marco Rubio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Rubio)___ , and South Carolina senator ___E:Tim Scott U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Scott)___ were finalists to be Trump's running mate.  Trump's two eldest sons, ___E:Donald Trump Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump_Jr.)___ and ___E:Eric Trump U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Trump)___ , advocated for Vance.

Several media and industry figures are said to have lobbied for Vance to be on the ticket, including ___E:Elon Musk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elon_Musk)___ , ___E:David O. Sacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_O._Sacks)___ , ___E:Tucker Carlson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tucker_Carlson)___ , and ___E:Peter Thiel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Thiel)___ , who first introduced Trump to Vance in 2021.   ___E:The Heritage Foundation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Heritage_Foundation)___ , which drafted ___E:Project 2025 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_2025)___ , privately advocated for Vance.
Musk responded to Trump's vice-presidential pick hours after its announcement, saying the ticket "resounds with victory".

David Sacks, a prominent GOP donor and Silicon Valley venture capitalist, wrote on Twitter: "This is who I want by Trump's side: an American patriot." In 2022, Sacks gave a ___E:super PAC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_action_committee)___ supporting Vance's Senate campaign $900,000, and Thiel added $15 million.
It was initially reported that Musk would contribute $45 million monthly to the Trump-Vance campaign,  but Musk later said he planned to donate "much lower amounts".
On May 15, 2024, Trump attended a $50,000 per head private fundraising dinner with Vance in ___E:Cincinnati U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati)___ .
Guests included ___E:Chris Bortz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Bortz)___ and Republican fundraiser ___E:Nate Morris U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nate_Morris)___ .
Vance appeared at significant conservative political events and in June was described as a potential running mate for Trump.

In July, a former friend of Vance's from Yale Law School exposed to the media communications between them and Vance from 2014 to 2017, with the friend alleging that Vance has "changed [his] opinion on literally every imaginable issue that affects everyday Americans" in pursuit of "political power and wealth".

In late July 2024, after President ___E:Joe Biden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden)___ ___E:withdrew his candidacy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withdrawal_of_Joe_Biden_from_the_2024_United_States_presidential_election)___ for ___E:reelection U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden_2024_presidential_campaign)___ and Vice President ___E:Kamala Harris U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris)___ became a ___E:presidential candidate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris_2024_presidential_campaign)___ , Vance said at a private fundraiser that the "bad news is that Kamala Harris does not have the same baggage as Joe Biden ...

Kamala Harris is obviously not struggling in the same ways that Joe Biden did"; a day later, Vance told the media: "I don't think the political calculus changes at all" whether Harris or Biden was the Democratic nominee.

Following criticism of his past remarks and political positions, Vance said in an August 2024 interview that a vice president "doesn't really matter" and that "Kamala Harris has been a bad vice president".
This came after Trump said that the "vice president, in terms of the election, does not have any impact".

In late August, after the Trump campaign was embroiled in controversy for allegedly bringing cameras into a restricted area of ___E:Arlington National Cemetery U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_National_Cemetery)___ during Trump's visit there, Vance first said that Harris "can go to hell" because "she wants to yell at Donald Trump because he showed up", and then said "Don't do this fake outrage thing".
At the time of his comments, Harris had not publicly discussed the ___E:incident U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump_2024_presidential_campaign#Arlington_National_Cemetery_incident)___ .

In August 2024, Vance said that Trump had "said that explicitly that he would" veto a national abortion ban.  In September 2024, during his debate with Harris, Trump was asked about Vance's statement about the veto, and responded: "I didn't discuss it with JD ...
I think he was speaking for me—but I really didn't."

On February 28, 2025, Vance and Trump met Ukrainian President ___E:Volodymyr Zelenskyy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volodymyr_Zelenskyy)___ in the White House's Oval Office in front of journalists in an internationally broadcast event.
Vance was mostly quiet for the meeting's first 40 minutes, but then interjected to answer a question about Trump's relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Vance told Zelenskyy: "The path to peace and the path to prosperity is maybe engaging in diplomacy ...
What makes America a good country is America engaging in diplomacy.

That's what President Trump is doing."  Zelenskyy responded that Putin had not abided by a ceasefire and prisoner exchange agreement with Ukraine, and asked Vance, "What kind of diplomacy, JD, you are speaking about?"

The conversation became hostile; Vance replied that he was discussing "diplomacy that's going to end the destruction of" Ukraine, telling Zelenskyy: "it's disrespectful for you to come to the Oval Office and try to litigate this in front of the American media.
Right now, you guys are going around and forcing conscripts to the front lines because you have manpower problems.

You should be thanking the president for trying to bring an end to this conflict."   Zelenskyy asked whether Vance had ever visited Ukraine; Vance replied that he had "watched and seen the stories" about Ukraine, accusing Zelenskyy of showing a "propaganda tour" of Ukraine.
He asked whether Zelenskyy had ever offered thanks, despite Zelenskyy starting the conversation by saying "Thank you so much" to Trump.

Vance incorrectly claimed that Zelenskyy "went to Pennsylvania and campaigned for the opposition in October" 2024; Zelenskyy had actually visited a factory to thank workers producing ammunition for Ukraine,  though the timing of the visit and separately calling Vance "too radical" raised suspicion among Republicans.
After the meeting, Zelenskyy and his delegation were made to leave the White House, canceling the original plan to sign a minerals deal between Ukraine and the U.S.
